analysis.one_liner: Gives the FDA power to order safety studies, restrict, or pull risky drugs from the market, and protects FDA whistleblowers.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee in July 2006, never received a committee vote or a floor vote, and died when the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007, with zero cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have let the Secretary of Health and Human Services order safety studies of already-approved drugs when new evidence raised concerns, and restrict how those drugs are distributed or advertised while the studies run. New drugs approved on preliminary evidence would have carried labels warning that approval was conditional, and companies that skipped required studies or labeling changes would have faced civil penalties of up to 100 percent of the drug's gross profits. It also would have made it illegal to punish FDA employees for reporting safety problems or fraud, and given FDA scientists the right to publish their findings.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who take prescription drugs. The bill was written in the wake of drugs like Vioxx being pulled from the market years after approval: it would have made the FDA move within 30 days when new safety evidence surfaced, forced companies to finish the follow-up studies they promise at approval, put warning labels on drugs approved only conditionally, and fined companies up to 100 percent of a drug's gross profits for ignoring study or labeling requirements. FDA employees who spot safety problems would have gained protection from retaliation and the right to publish what they find.

how_it_helps.text: It lets the Secretary of Health and Human Services order companies to run postmarket studies when evidence of a safety or effectiveness problem emerges, and to restrict how a suspect drug is distributed, prescribed, or advertised while the study runs.

It requires companies to complete promised follow-up studies as a condition of approving new drugs, and lets the FDA withdraw a drug from the market if the study results are inconclusive or the study is never finished.

It creates civil penalties for selling misbranded drugs or failing to complete required postmarket studies — up to 100 percent of the sponsor's gross profits from the drug, rising to 300 percent if a consumer is harmed.

It protects FDA employees who report illegal activity, fraud, or threats to public health from being fired, demoted, or otherwise punished, with reinstatement, back pay, and punitive damages available to those who prevail.
It gives FDA scientists an unwaivable right to publish their findings in scientific journals, so government researchers can share safety data publicly.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers. They would have faced mandatory postmarket studies, possible restrictions on distribution and advertising, mandatory warning labels on conditionally approved drugs, civil penalties reaching 100 percent of a drug's gross profits (300 percent if a consumer was harmed), and liability for retaliating against employees who report problems. Some patients with serious illnesses might also have faced slower access to drugs approved on preliminary evidence, since distribution would be restricted until follow-up studies were done.

drawbacks.text: The bill would have restricted access to drugs approved under the accelerated-approval process: it allowed distribution limits, restricted advertising, and required labels warning that a drug 'will not receive full approval until completion of further testing' — slowing access for patients with serious conditions who accept uncertainty in exchange for a chance at benefit.

Civil penalties were set at up to 100 percent of a drug's gross profits (300 percent if a consumer is harmed), which even supporters would acknowledge is a sweeping penalty structure that could discourage investment in new drugs.

If a required postmarket study was not finished within eight years, the results would be presumed inconclusive and the drug pulled from general sale — a hard deadline that may not fit how long real-world studies actually take.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits were substantial: faster government action on unsafe drugs, real penalties for stalling safety studies, honest labels on conditionally approved drugs, and protection for FDA scientists who speak up. The costs were real but narrower: slower access to some experimental drugs for seriously ill patients who accept risk, and penalty amounts so large that even supporters would call them aggressive. On balance the bill was a consumer-safety measure whose main risk was overcorrection, and it never received even a committee vote, so neither its benefits nor its costs were ever tested.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Health Subcommittee in the summer of 2006 and no one ever scheduled it for a hearing or a vote, so it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Edward Markey introduced the bill on July 27, 2006, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
On August 1, 2006, it was referred to the committee's Subcommittee on Health, which was its final action; no hearing, markup, or vote ever followed.
No other member of the House signed on as a cosponsor.
The 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007, and bills not passed by then expire.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug makers were better off: they faced no new postmarket study mandates, no distribution or advertising restrictions, no gross-profit-based penalties, and no new whistleblower exposure. Patients, meanwhile, got no new safety protections.

for.name: Rep. Edward Markey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the SAFE Drug Act on July 27, 2006 and delivered introductory remarks on the House floor.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. Joe Barton (R-TX)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on July 27, 2006 and never scheduled the bill for a hearing, markup, or vote; its last action was a secondary referral to the Subcommittee on Health on August 1, 2006.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Democratic sponsor and no cosponsors of either party, so it never drew a party-line fight; it died in committee without any recorded vote.

industries.note: The bill would have subjected their drugs to mandatory postmarket studies, possible distribution and advertising restrictions, mandatory warning labels on conditionally approved drugs, and civil penalties of up to 100 percent of gross profits (300 percent if a consumer is harmed). Its interest in avoiding these requirements ran against the public's interest in knowing a drug works before it stays on the market.

industries.industry: Employers of potential whistleblowers (including drug companies and their contractors)
industries.note: The bill made it unlawful to punish employees for reporting violations or health threats to regulators, Congress, or supervisors, and allowed large awards including punitive damages up to $5 million. Companies could no longer rely on employees staying quiet about safety problems.
